# sysutils_sudoers (Resource)

Manages a sudo drop-in file in `/etc/sudoers.d`, below the provider's `root_dir` if that is set. The file is written atomically with mode `0440` and owned by `root:root`, and is checked with `visudo -cf` before it is renamed into place, so that a syntax error never locks everyone out of sudo. It is removed on destroy. Requires root privileges.

It covers the same ground as Ansible's `community.general.sudoers` module, or a `template` task with `validate: visudo -cf %s`. Each resource owns one file, `/etc/sudoers.d/<name>`.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# Written to /etc/sudoers.d/50-deploy:
#
#   # Managed by Terraform (sysutils_sudoers). Manual changes will be reverted.
#   %deploy ALL = (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart app.service, /usr/bin/systemctl reload nginx.service
#   alice ALL = (ALL:ALL) ALL
resource "sysutils_sudoers" "deploy" {
  name = "50-deploy"

  rules = [
    {
      users    = ["%deploy"]
      runas    = "root"
      nopasswd = true
      commands = [
        "/usr/bin/systemctl restart app.service",
        "/usr/bin/systemctl reload nginx.service",
      ]
    },
    {
      users    = ["alice"]
      runas    = "ALL:ALL"
      commands = ["ALL"]
    },
  ]
}

# Anything sudoers can express, written verbatim. visudo checks the file
# before it is installed, so a typo fails the apply instead of breaking sudo.
resource "sysutils_sudoers" "backup" {
  name    = "60-backup"
  content = <<-EOT
    Defaults:backup !requiretty, env_keep += "BORG_PASSPHRASE"
    Cmnd_Alias BACKUP = /usr/bin/rsync, /usr/bin/borg
    backup ALL = (root) NOPASSWD: BACKUP
  EOT
}
```

## Schema

### Required

- `name` (String) Name of the file in `/etc/sudoers.d`, such as `"90-deploy"`. Must not contain `.` or `/`, white space or control characters, and must not end with `~`: sudo silently skips files in `sudoers.d` whose names contain a `.` or end with `~`. Changing this forces a new resource.

### Optional

- `content` (String) Contents of the file, in sudoers syntax, written verbatim. Exactly one of `content` and `rules` must be set; with `rules`, this is the rendered file. Refresh reads the file, so any change made outside Terraform shows up as a planned change to this attribute.
- `rules` (Attributes List) User specifications to write instead of `content`, one line each, after a line saying that the file is managed by Terraform: `<users> <hosts> = (<runas>) NOPASSWD: SETENV: <commands>`. Exactly one of `content` and `rules` must be set. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--rules))
- `validate` (Boolean) Whether to check the new file with `visudo -cf` before it is installed. If visudo rejects it, apply fails with visudo's output and the file on disk is left as it was. On the host, visudo must then be installed. Below the provider's `root_dir`, the check is skipped with a warning if the tree has no `visudo`, or if the host running Terraform has none to run: programs in the tree are never run. Defaults to `true`.

### Read-Only

- `group` (String) Group of the file; always the group with GID 0 (`"root"`) after apply. A different group on disk shows up as drift.
- `id` (String) Resource identifier (equal to `name`).
- `mode` (String) Mode of the file; always `"0440"` after apply. A different mode on disk shows up as drift.
- `owner` (String) Owner of the file; always `"root"` after apply. A different owner on disk shows up as drift.
- `path` (String) Path of the file, `/etc/sudoers.d/<name>`.

<a id="nestedatt--rules"></a>
### Nested Schema for `rules`

Required:

- `commands` (List of String) Commands the users may run, such as `"/usr/bin/systemctl restart app"`, `"sudoedit /etc/app.conf"` or `"ALL"`. Each element must be a single command: `,`, `:` and `=` in arguments must be escaped with a backslash (`"\\,"` in HCL), as sudoers requires.
- `users` (List of String) Who the rule applies to: user names, `%group`, `#uid`, `%#gid`, `+netgroup`, user aliases or `ALL`, each prefixed with `!` to exclude it. Elements must not contain white space, `,`, `=`, `:` or parentheses.

Optional:

- `hosts` (List of String) Hosts the rule applies on: host names, addresses, networks, `+netgroup`, host aliases or `ALL`. Defaults to `["ALL"]`.
- `nopasswd` (Boolean) Whether the commands may be run without a password (`NOPASSWD:`). Defaults to `false`.
- `runas` (String) Who the commands may be run as, written in parentheses: `"ALL"`, `"ALL:ALL"`, `"postgres"` or `":docker"` (users, then groups after a `:`). If unset, the commands may only be run as root.
- `setenv` (Boolean) Whether the user may keep environment variables that sudo would otherwise remove (`SETENV:`). Defaults to `false`.

## The Drop-in File

Set exactly one of `content` and `rules`:

- `content` is written verbatim. Use it for anything the structured rules can't express, such as `Defaults`, aliases or `@include`.
- `rules` renders one user specification per rule, after a line saying that the file is managed by Terraform.

The first example above writes:

```
# Managed by Terraform (sysutils_sudoers). Manual changes will be reverted.
%deploy ALL = (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart app.service, /usr/bin/systemctl reload nginx.service
alice ALL = (ALL:ALL) ALL
```

Every field of a rule is checked at plan time so that it can only say what it appears to say: `users` and `hosts` elements can't contain `,`, `=`, `:`, parentheses or white space, `runas` can't contain parentheses, and a command can't contain an unescaped `,`, `:` or `=`, which sudoers would read as the start of another command or user specification. No field can contain a newline or end with a backslash, which would continue the line.

The file is written like the other files of the provider: to a temporary file in `/etc/sudoers.d` whose name starts with `.`, so that sudo ignores it, which is then renamed into place. Readers see either the old or the new file, never a partial one. The file always gets mode `0440` and owner `root:root`, whatever they were before, and they are set before any content is written, so there is never a moment in which anyone but root could change the file. Extended attributes such as the SELinux label are carried over; an ACL is dropped. A missing `/etc/sudoers.d` is created with mode `0750`.

## Validation with visudo

A syntax error in any file sudo reads makes sudo refuse to run at all, which can lock every administrator out of a host. With `validate = true`, the default, the complete temporary file, already with its final mode and owner, is therefore checked with `visudo -cf` before it is renamed into place:

- If visudo rejects it, apply fails with an `Invalid sudoers file` error that contains visudo's output, with the temporary file's name replaced by the drop-in's path, and the temporary file is deleted. The file on disk, and the state, stay exactly as they were, so the previous rules keep working; a new drop-in is not created at all.
- visudo checks only the new file, not how it combines with the rest of the sudoers configuration. For example, an alias defined in another file is accepted, with a warning that it is not defined in the drop-in.
- On the host, visudo must be installed; otherwise apply fails and asks you to install sudo or set `validate = false`. It is looked up in the provider's `PATH` and run with `LC_ALL=C` and a 30-second timeout.
- Below the provider's `root_dir`, the provider never runs programs from the tree. If the tree contains `visudo` (in `/usr/local/sbin`, `/usr/local/bin`, `/usr/sbin`, `/usr/bin`, `/sbin` or `/bin`), the host's visudo checks the file. If the tree has no visudo, sudo is presumably not installed there, and if the host has none to run, the check is skipped and apply succeeds with a `sudoers file not validated` warning. Install sudo in the tree before writing its drop-ins, or set `validate = false` to silence the warning.

With `validate = false` the file is installed unchecked.

## Behavior

- **Create** refuses to overwrite an existing file of the same name, such as one installed by a package: destroying the resource would delete it. Import the file instead, or remove it.
- **Update** rewrites and re-validates the file. Changing `name` replaces the resource, which removes the old file.
- **Destroy** removes the file. If something other than a regular file, such as a symlink, is at the path, destroy fails and leaves it alone.

sudo reads its configuration on every invocation, so changes take effect immediately; there is nothing to reload.

## File Names

sudo's `@includedir` (or `#includedir`) directive silently skips files whose names contain a `.` or end with `~`, so that editor backups and package manager leftovers such as `admins.dpkg-old` are never read. A drop-in named `admins.conf` would therefore be written, validated and then ignored by sudo. `name` is checked at plan time and must not contain `.` or `/` (it names a file directly in `/etc/sudoers.d`), white space or control characters, and must not end with `~`. Files are read in lexical order, so a numeric prefix such as `50-deploy` controls which of several drop-ins wins where they conflict.

## Drift Detection

On refresh the provider reads the file:

- `content` holds the whole file, so any change made outside Terraform, including lines added by hand, shows up as a planned change of `content`, and the next apply restores the file. With `rules`, the plan compares the file with the rendered rules.
- `mode`, `owner` and `group` hold the file's actual mode and ownership, so a file made writable or given to another user plans an update back to `0440` and `root:root`.
- If the file has been deleted, the resource is removed from the state and the next apply creates it again. If something other than a regular file (such as a symlink) is at the path, refresh fails rather than following it.

## Import

An existing drop-in can be imported by the name of its file in `/etc/sudoers.d`:

```shell
# By the name of the file in /etc/sudoers.d. The file's contents become
# content; rules are left unset.
terraform import sysutils_sudoers.backup 60-backup
```

The file's contents are imported as `content`, and `validate` is set to `true`. A configuration with the same `content` plans no change. A configuration with `rules` plans an update to the rendered file unless it is identical, including the header line.

## Caveats

- The resource requires root, both to write to `/etc/sudoers.d` and to own the file as root.
- sudo only reads `/etc/sudoers.d` if `/etc/sudoers` includes it with `@includedir /etc/sudoers.d` (or the older `#includedir`). The stock sudoers of Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL and Alpine do. The provider does not change `/etc/sudoers`; use a [`sysutils_file_line`](./file_line.md) to add the line where it is missing.
- `users` and `hosts` are not checked for existence. Reference a [`sysutils_user`](./user.md) or [`sysutils_group`](./group.md) resource to order the two.
- Commands must be absolute paths (or `ALL`, `sudoedit` or an alias); visudo rejects relative ones.
- With the provider's `root_dir` argument set, the file is written to `etc/sudoers.d` below `root_dir`, for example to grant sudo rights in an image being built; see [Validation with visudo](#validation-with-visudo). Symlinks in the tree are resolved inside it, as for `sysutils_file`; `path` stays the path inside the root.
- Concurrent edits of the same drop-in, from this or another Terraform run, are serialised with the provider's file lock.
